summary: Describes ISAKMP, a framework for establishing, negotiating, modifying and deleting security associations and the cryptographic keys that go with them. It defines message formats and procedures rather than a specific key exchange. It is now historic, replaced by RFC 4306.

eli5.summary: Before two people can whisper secrets, they must agree on a code. ISAKMP is the set of rules for how computers agree on the code and swap the keys.

questions: what is internet security association and key management protocol
how do two systems negotiate security
subtitle: Framework for negotiating security agreements and exchanging cryptographic keys.

tldr.problem: Before two systems can communicate securely, they must agree on which encryption and authentication methods to use, and exchange the keys needed to protect their traffic. Different applications need different security services.
tldr.mechanism: ISAKMP defines a framework for peers to negotiate security associations (agreements about how to protect traffic) independently from specific key exchange methods. It uses a two-phase approach: first establishing a protected channel between the peers, then using that channel to negotiate security for the actual data traffic.
tldr.outcome: Systems can dynamically negotiate compatible security policies and keys without hardcoding algorithms, supporting diverse security requirements. It is now historic and has been superseded by RFC 4306.

today: RFC 4306 (IKEv1) superseded this document, consolidating ISAKMP and key exchange specifications into a single protocol. RFC 2408 is now historic, though the concepts of security associations and the two-phase model remain central to IPsec, GDOI, and other key management protocols.

sections.title: Why Negotiation Matters
sections.content:
The Internet has many ways to protect data: different encryption algorithms (DES, AES), different authentication methods (RSA signatures, Kerberos), and different key exchange techniques. A single organization might require one type of security inside its private network, a different type to communicate with customers, and yet another for government contracts. ISAKMP lets each party offer the security methods it supports and agree on a common choice, rather than requiring every pair of systems to pre-arrange their security.

ISAKMP also separates security association management (what rules will govern this conversation) from key exchange (how to share the actual keys). This separation lets organizations choose any key exchange method that suits them while using a common protocol to agree on the details.
sections.eli5: Different groups of people might want to use different secret codes: your family might like one code, your school another, and your sports team a third. Instead of everyone learning every code, ISAKMP lets you say "which codes do you know?" and pick one you both know.

sections.title: Security Associations
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a contract between two systems that specifies how they will protect their traffic. It includes the encryption algorithm, the authentication method, the key length, and other parameters. The SA is identified by a Security Parameter Index (SPI), a number that points to the right set of rules.

ISAKMP uses a two-phase model. In Phase 1, the two systems establish their own ISAKMP SA, creating a protected channel. Then in Phase 2, they use that protected channel to negotiate SAs for other protocols (like IPsec). This approach amortizes the cost of authentication: the expensive cryptographic work happens once in Phase 1, and then multiple Phase 2 negotiations use the same protected channel without repeating it.
sections.eli5: An SA is like a contract that says "we will use this code and this key." The SPI is a number you write on the envelope so the other side knows which contract you mean. Phase 1 gets you to trust each other, then Phase 2 uses that trust to agree on what code to use for your actual messages.

sections.title: Messages and Payloads
sections.content:
ISAKMP messages have a fixed header (28 bytes) followed by variable payloads. The header contains two 8-byte cookies (anti-clogging tokens), the exchange type, flags, a message ID, and the total message length. Payloads are modular components that carry specific information: the Security Association payload describes an SA; the Key Exchange payload contains the initiator's public key information; the Identification payload names the sender; the Certificate payload provides cryptographic credentials; the Hash payload proves the sender knows the shared secret.

ISAKMP defines 13 payload types, each with a generic header followed by type-specific data. Multiple payloads can be stacked in a single message, and the next-payload field chains them together. The receiver uses the exchange type (from the header) to know which payloads to expect in which messages.
sections.eli5: An ISAKMP message is like a letter with a standard envelope. The envelope always has the same fields: who sent it, who it is for, what kind of message it is, and how long it is. Inside the envelope are smaller envelopes, each carrying one piece of information.

sections.title: Exchange Types
sections.content:
An exchange type is a sequence of messages that achieves a specific security goal. ISAKMP defines four Phase 1 exchange types: Base Exchange (4 messages, no identity protection), Identity Protection Exchange (6 messages, protects the peers' names), Authentication Only Exchange (3 messages, for systems that already share credentials), and Aggressive Exchange (3 messages, faster but less secure). Each exchange type uses a different sequence of payloads to provide different protections against different attacks.

The exchange type determines the number of round trips, which payloads are sent in each message, and in what order. A system can support multiple exchange types and choose the right one based on its local policy and what the peer offers.
sections.eli5: An exchange type is a dance step: different dances have different moves (some are 3 steps, some are 6 steps), and each move reveals different information about the dancers at different times. A faster dance might let everyone see your face right away, while a slower dance keeps your identity hidden until you are both ready.

sections.title: Protection Against Attacks
sections.content: ISAKMP protects against several categories of attacks. Cookies (anti-clogging tokens) are generated with the initiator's IP address, port, and a random secret, making it impossible for an attacker to obtain a valid cookie without contacting the real responder; this prevents attackers from overwhelming the server with forged requests. The state machine ensures that missing or out-of-order messages will not create an incomplete SA; if a required message is missing, the protocol restarts. Strong authentication using digital signatures (not shared passwords) ensures that the SA is established with the intended peer, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. The linking of ISAKMP exchanges prevents an attacker from completing authentication and then impersonating a peer during the key exchange.
sections.eli5: ISAKMP has several bodyguards: a cookie checks that you are the real recipient; a sequence check makes sure messages arrive in order; a signature proves you are who you say you are. Together they make it very hard for someone to sneak in and pretend to be the other person.

sections.title: Overview of the Framework
sections.content:
ISAKMP is a framework, not a complete protocol. It specifies the message structure, the exchange types, and the processing rules, but it does not mandate a specific key exchange algorithm or encryption method. Each Domain of Interpretation (DOI) fills in these details: the Internet IP Security DOI (defined in RFC 2407) specifies which algorithms are allowed for IPsec, which payload formats to use, and how to name the algorithms. Other DOIs can be defined for other protocols.

The RFC was published in November 1998 as an Internet Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 4306 (IKEv1 reformulated), which consolidated ISAKMP with the key exchange specifics. However, ISAKMP concepts remain foundational to IPsec and group key management protocols like GDOI.
sections.eli5: ISAKMP is like a cookbook that says "here is how to write a recipe: start with these ingredients, follow these steps, and everyone will understand it." But it does not say "you must use salt and pepper." Other rules define which ingredients (algorithms) you are allowed to use.
